subtopic: WELFARE BENEFITS TO WOMEN RETURNING TO RESERVES

speechtext:
Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of
Citizenship and Immigration): Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity of announcing two policy decisions concerning the administration of Indian affairs.
The first concerns women of Indian origin who have lost their Indian status through enfranchisement or marriage, and who have no alternative but to return to friends and relatives on the reserves for various reasons such as the death of their husbands or serious illness in the family.
Up to the present there has been no satisfactory means whereby essential welfare and educational help could be provided to these women and their children. It has been decided, therefore, on humanitarian grounds that educational and welfare assistance shall be granted to these people on reserves in the same manner and to the same extent as though they had Indian status.
Second, I wish to announce that the federal government is prepared to negotiate agreements with the governments of the various provinces for the extension of normal provincial welfare services to persons residing on Indian reserves. The purpose is to avoid the development of exclusive welfare services on reserves which would tend to set Indians apart from other Canadians and duplicate provincial programs in adjacent non-Indian communities.
In negotiating these agreements the federal government is prepared to pay a reasonable share of the costs of the benefits, over and above the federal contribution under existing federal-provincial agreements, such as the Unemployment Assistance Act; and to share with the provinces reasonable costs of additional staff and administration required for the application of such programs. Moreover, my department will be prepared to enter into agreements to enable Indian bands to assume responsibilities for welfare programs normally administered by municipalities under provincial legislation.

subtopic: WELFARE BENEFITS TO WOMEN RETURNING TO RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. lady on both these
announcements. I think they are both very progressive steps indeed.

speechtext: We also appreciate the announcements made by the minister with respect to these two matters, which are exceptionally good ones. We hope additional steps will be taken later on in order to deal with other similar problems.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CONFERENCE ON LAW OF THE SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. gentleman knows, from time to time in order to attain a reasonable measure of agreement without the sacrifice of rights that are regarded as first principles, changes are necessarily made. The conference has been proceeding for some time, and the Canadian government has concluded that it is most desirable without the sacrifice of principles, to attain a measure of agreement which has been attempted for many years.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker; Mr. Morrison was paroled last night. Information I received this morning indicates that this fact was communicated to the authorities in Nova Scotia by telegram last night, and the certificate of parole is being forwarded to Hamilton where Mr. Morrison was employed and to which place he wishes to return.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
As I was saying, we have the right- and without unduly interfering with the internal business of the C.B.C.-to try to establish some relationship between what the C.B.C. is costing the taxpayers and the quality of what it is offering to them. That is the point of view I had adopted during the inquiry of the committee on broadcasting, and it is in the same spirit I should like to make the following remarks.
The C.B.C. is not a public service, in the same way as are certain other government bodies. Its services are of a moral category, because they have a direct bearing on the souls and minds of our citizens.

The Budget-Mr. Tremblay
Therefore, we cannot, in regard to any C.B.C. activities, use the same criteria we are accustomed to use in the case of activities of an ordinary crown corporation. It is not surprising, therefore, that the members of the parliamentary committee should have tried to go beyond the requirements of an inquiry into purely administrative and financial matters.
For my part, I tried to define the problem in its exact terms, and to establish what must, first of all, constitute the basis of the C.B.C., its purposes, its principles, its methods, its means and the pertinent facts connected with what I have just outlined. I distinctly remember the wry faces of some C.B.C. pundits when we asked them what the C.B.C. should be, and about its responsibilities in the intellectual and moral field.
Their answer was that the C.B.C. was trying to provide wholesome and entertaining programs. That was a very neat way of begging the question.
Yet, in putting those questions, the members were trying to echo the representations made by the public. They were asking, on behalf of others, the essential questions. They were making their own the opinions, criticisms and protests of the people whom it is their duty to represent. I do not think we can decently challenge the validity of such representations on the part of the people. They are the democratic expression of a right, based on democratic principles and on the normal exercise of democratic privileges. Those who think that the legitimate representatives of the people have nothing to do with the claims of those who have elected them and who, through their taxes, are paying for the administration of the C.B.C., show utter contempt for democracy, in whose name they are none the less pursuing all their destructive campaigns.
I think Mr. Speaker, that we have a right to examine all the facts pertaining to the administration of the C.B.C. We have such a right because the people have recognized it in appointing us to represent them and to defend their interests in this house. We would be derelict in our duty if we evaded such a difficult and thankless task. We have a right to inquire into the cost of the C.B.C., because it is the people who are paying and because we are the official representatives of the people.
We also have a right to look into the ethics of the C.B.C., in order to assess the value

of its program policies, and find out whether the C.B.C. is carrying out the purposes for which it was set up, and whether its activities are truly in line with the needs of the human community it is designed to serve.
I think some people fail to realize the importance of these basic problems, and tend to minimize the role of the people's representatives.
We are a legitimate government and as such, the trustees of the public welfare. We have the rights that correspond to that tremendous responsibility. There is an essential democratic principle involved here.
I have had occasions in the past to commend the C.B.C. in this house. I then had in mind certain high quality productions which deserve the highest praise. That is no reason why I should not criticize its other productions, whether of medium or of poor quality, and to judge them severely in view of what the taxpayer has to pay.
I recognize that, in this field as in others, no one can be perfect. Still, there are certain mistakes that should never be made, when the people are footing the bill. There are basic rules of caution which must be observed so as to keep to a minimum the risks involved in necessary experiments. To quote just one example, take the case of the broadcasting of the production: "La plus Belle de Ceans". It cost the taxpayers $84,000. No one has ever denied it was a failure. A failure which was due, in the very words of Mr. Marcel Ouimet, to a "slackening of the usual supervisory machinery", which in plain English, means a lack of elementary supervision and precautions. Apart from its cost, it was a major blunder, considering the circumstances. Could anyone be surprised, therefore, that protests poured in after the broadcast, that an investigation was demanded, and that it was even urged that those responsible be fired for such a gross mistake, if we can so describe it, in view of the circumstances, the context and the atmosphere surrounding the event? Hardly anyone could be found, except the author of "La Vertu des Chattes" (The tabby-cat's virtue) to shield the responsible parties. Then finally a C.B.C. representative, Mr. Gerard Lamarche, summed up the situation by saying that if the C.B.C. sometimes blunders, it never does so deliberately.
Now, Mr. Speaker, you know why roses are red and violets are blue. This is the very height of justification. As if it were

conceivable, in a field like the C.B.C. that people might goof with intent. I can't make head or tail of it, although I can see that the C.B.C., unaccustomed as it is to account for its deeds and misdeeds, has not yet hit upon the standard phrases and blanket alibis.
But reverting to my subject, I maintain that we were entitled, without underestimating the importance of the work done by the C.B.C., nor attempting to whittle down its public prestige or to discredit anyone, we were entitled, as I say, to have the C.B.C. account for itself. All the more so because the deficits piled up by the C.B.C. are forcing us to seek new funds from the taxpayers. I therefore feel no embarrassment in availing myself of representations made by the people to direct questions to the C.B.C. on its general policy, on its plans, on the philosophy behind its information activities, its recreational programs and on what it describes as its educational broadcasts, because I have received such representations from known public bodies, educational institutions, associations, religious societies, and individuals in all walks of life, all of whom are justly alarmed at the philosophy apparently prevailing in the C.B.C., which disregards the traditional and historical values of the Canadian community.
I do not think I am wrong in following up, in that matter, the directives of the bishops of the civil province of Quebec, who voiced serious and significant protests about the French network. My reason for speaking today is to give expression once again to all those representations, and to those which were made last summer by a group of citizens who met in Montreal to discuss the problems of our government radio and television systems.
May I take this opportunity to express astonishment at the fact that our friends of the Liberal party did not deem it necessary to file a strong protest against the program I mentioned a while ago, and at the fact that they did not comment on the episcopal collective letter. Their only steps were those in defence of the three gentlemen of the English network who took it into their heads one day, in order to protect their meagre fees, to stir up a war against what they called political interference, which, in any case, they could never prove. Nothing else mattered, no, neither the philosophy of the C.B.C., the intellectual as well as the moral dangers of some programs nor the slant of its information. All of a sudden, Messrs. Peers, Gillis
The Budget-Mr. Tremblay and Trotter of Toronto were the C.B.C., with a Montreal branch run by Laurendeau and Gagnon. Let us recognize, Mr. Speaker, that we ran a great risk in that case, and that Canada as a whole was never closer to a catastrophe. The point was this: those men were resigning because they were no longer allowed their daily gravy, so miserably earned by their few minutes of commentaries every morning. Without that breeze from Toronto each morning, the nation would wither away. An executive's weakness removed the threat, the program was resumed and Messrs. Gagnon and Laurendeau did not have to resign and actually were saved from an embarrassing financial flop.
The moral of this story is that the government has no right to raise its voice in criticism, be it a shadow of criticism. The people's representatives have no right to complain about the huge costs of the C.B.C., they have no right to say that programs of questionable quality are costing huge amounts; even less are they allowed to think that slanted information is a bad thing. No, this is all political interference. The result is that we accept the existence of a state within the state, and that our sole recognized right is the right to vote money to a corporation without knowing exactly what use is being made of it.
Mr. Speaker, I say that the rights and privileges of the C.B.C. are those which are granted and recognized by parliament, that this parliament has the right to demand an accounting and that the members of parliament have the right, like other citizens, and on behalf of the citizens they represent, to complain about the C.B.C. Otherwise we are allowing the establishment of feudal benefice, of game preserves, which sooner or later become a burden upon the state and a threat to its security. The Canada Council, if you allow me to say so, is becoming that type of mighty organization which disclaims any responsibility towards parliament.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is true.

speechtext:
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that if we allow the setting up of such organizations, we are endangering the rights of parliament and democratic privileges. The people of Canada are forced to accept institutions which they are called upon to maintain and provide for, but which do not accept corresponding obligations towards the people.
Those are the views I put forward last year in the committee on broadcasting. I have tried to uphold the principles of a responsible government. Moreover, I feel this is the purpose for which the committees of the house are set up, so that from time to time the members may have the opportunity to

The Budget-Mr. Tremblay analyse in detail the administration they entrust to officials. Thus, the members in turn are in a position to account to the public, to explain the machinery of administration and to justify the expenditures so incurred.
I repeat that the committee on broadcasting could not perform its duties. It has been more or less a smokescreen, because it did not have the means to get the necessary information. The discussions were hampered with all kinds of technicalities of procedure. I do not hesitate to say also that the French speaking members did not have the opportunity to go into a full and detailed study of the French network administration.
Therefore, I regret that this committee has not been re-established sooner. Needless to say that what has been announced in that regard-that is, that we would be studying instead the problems of private stations- could not satisfy those who believe that before judging private enterprise and setting up rules and regulations for it, we should first settle the affairs of the government owned corporation.
I feel that the public radio network is costing the taxpayers enough money to justify us in trying, first of all, to clarify the situation there. If we can manage to restore to it an inspiration and a policy in conformity with its objectives and aims, then we shall be able to hold it as an example and use it as a model, for who can claim that it has really improved?
The complaints made by the public last year still stand. We might even say that the C.B.C. has tightened certain policies and seems to challenge public opinion. Mr. Alphonse Ouimet, its president, took the lead when he announced certain changes- changes of form at the most, aimed at fooling the public-in the management of the corporation.
In an interview with Mr. Claude Paulette, on October 1, 1959, during the T.V. news program at 11 o'clock at night, he did not hesitate to say that the recommendations of the committee on broadcasting had nothing to do with the changes he was announcing.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote what was said during that interview which is really, as will be seen, a masterpiece of insolence:

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

It was quite a blow. The patient had really recovered; he had all the strength needed to jeer at the minister responsible for the C.B.C., at the government and at members of parliament.
This explains why known commentators were brought back so quickly, why our institutions were again the target of attacks, why anyone could say anything on the government owned radio or television network as long as his words bore the stamp of that spirit of anarchy that has been denounced on many occasions in certain circles.
There still prevails in the C.B.C. this amoral atmosphere consisting of a complete disregard of principles inspired by Catholic and Christian ethics; as in the case of the frequently harmful movies that are shown without any consideration for the education of the public for which they are intended, and for its ability to make necessary reservations. Still scheduled are certain T.V. serials that are an outrageous caricature of the life, morals and languages of French Canadians; others that are downright stupid, or padded versions of writings of merit, but now made devoid of all sense and significance. The odious program "Music Hall" is still running, as is the inept program "Coq a l'ane" and the unqualifiable "En premiere", where nothing but insipid scripts have been offered, most of them reflecting a sense of morbidity already too much in honour in the C.B.C. There are many other programs quite as questionable;

entertaining programs, would say Mr. Marcel Ouimet, but which promote a taste for the nonsensical and trifling, when they do not simply undermine authority, or principles and values worthy of the highest respect.

speechtext: Mr. Rumilly will like this.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And those gentlemen, last year, at the time of the strike, labelled this "French culture". I am all for culture, as long as it means the elimination of American-inspired programs, nonsense of all kinds, caricatures of our language, programs of questionable moral quality, and those young people's programs that prompt our young people to break free from parental authority as soon as possible and to seek entertainment outside the home. What will be left, after all that? Surely there are some excellent programs, but on the whole unfortunately, there are too few.
I shall have the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to come back to the specific matter of programs. I shall then be able to specify the general criticisms I have just made, because it is not my intention to cast reflection on those C.B.C. officials who are doing remarkable work with a scrupulous conscientiousness and in a spirit steeped in the best cultural traditions.
What I denounce is everything that is done under the sign of improvisation, of amateurism and incompetence, not to mention the motives of profit and commercialism that mark the activity of certain stars and of certain producers.
There is also inefficiency at the top. The accumulated and repeated deficits of the C.B.C. had already shown it up cm another plane. The C.B.C. programs are still more eloquent in this respect.
That is why I advocate early and drastic reforms in the whole structure of the crown corporation, providing:
1.	That a crown minister be directly responsible for that public body as well as for the national film board, and other cultural government bodies;
2.	That a deputy minister be especially appointed to serve as a liaison officer between the minister and the corporation;
3.	That an advisory committee be set up, composed of prominent personalities in the religious, educational, social, artistic, cultural and economic fields; which advisory com-
The Budget-Mr. Tremblay mittee would have to make a complete study of the corporation's program policy and, when needed, act as a board of censorship;
4.	That competitions be organized for the recruiting of performers of all kinds, in cooperation with the conservatory of music and drama of the province, schools of fine arts and the various artistic and cultural bodies of the province of Quebec;
5.	That competitions be organized for the selection of radio and television scripts, and that a jury, recruited among personalities of the literary and artistic world, be appointed to judge those scripts, in co-operation with the C.B.C. producers;
6.	That the annual budget of the C.B.C. be included in the estimates of government expenditures and thus be open to criticism by the taxpayers' legitimate representatives.
Those suggestions do not prevent me from hoping that, in the near future, the setting up of a provincial radio network may look after purely educational programs, in order to put an end to that further federal interference in provincial affairs, through the medium of the C.B.C.
Those suggestions, Mr. Speaker, could serve as a basis for reorganizing the C.B.C. I claim that they are the last word in the matter. However, I do think they deal with some of the most important aspects of the general problem. I realize there are difficulties involved; they will certainly be interpreted as an attempt to make the C.B.C. subservient to politics. I do not think that is the case, and such is not my intention; in any case, they would have the advantage of making plain civil servants out of the regular employees of the C.B.C.-in this I do not include performers and writers-and would allow the government to exercise closer control over the corporation's finances. Such a reorganization would in no way impede the C.B.C.'s really cultured and artistic activity. It would however guarantee a better control over a government organization which, under the guise of freedom of speech or of thought, must not be left to the whims or will of coteries which strive to thrust their views, feelings, ideas or prejudices upon the people. Instead of being some kind of a state within the state, the C.B.C. would become again what it should be, an organization representative of our environment and reflecting its philosophy, its principles, its social, religious, political, artistic and cultural life, its aspirations, its concerns and various trends of thought.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order to appreciate the full significance of this year's budget I thought it might be useful to study a few flashbacks of the important events which have not only challenged Canada's strength and ingenuity in the past but which indicate clearly the magnitude of the problems that Canadians of this generation will have to face. Everyone will agree, I believe, that since confederation tremendous economic, social and political changes have taken place within the boundaries of our country which are indicative of and comparable with similar changes in the world as a whole. The extremely rapid pace with which these changes have been made in our country and in the world is to my mind of particular significance, and should be foremost in our thinking with respect to what is to happen in the remaining 40 years of this century.
Since the turn of the century the pace of our economic and social evolution has accelerated, and has gained a momentum which in many respects is causing justified anxiety. The tempo of life is quickening and the concept of values has changed. Materialism in all levels of society, particularly on the North American continent, has reached the point of being the accepted criterion of economic, social and even political consideration. So far as transportation is concerned, the world has shrunk so that now we are but a few hours away from the farthest geographical point, and we are even engaged in conquering outer space. Economic and military isolationism is now unrealistic. Absolute sovereignty in now sacrificed for economic and national security. The concept of international trade has so evolved that it is causing us serious trade problems. The world is split into two opposing ideological camps, and continues to face the possibility of a disastrous economic war or incredibly horrible military suicide.
In spite of these very real and undeniable problems and challenges, Mr. Speaker, the government, after having undermined Canada's financial stability, could offer to the country nothing more than the undecided budget that the Minister of Finance brought down the other evening, and which is characteristic of the policy of this "we knew it all" government. There have been serious problems and challenges in the past, but they have not been solved by indecision. The first world war taught us that Canada would no longer be excluded from international conflicts in other areas of the world, and we also learned that Canada was not immune to world economic disturbances.


The economic depression of the 1930's was a challenge to Canada. In 1935, Mr. Speaker, did Mackenzie King ask the opposition what they would do under the circumstances, as the Prime Minister has done ever since he assumed office? No, Mr. Speaker; Mackenzie King launched into what was then a revolutionary and extensive social legislative program, which in fact was opposed in part by the Conservatives, with the result that all the social legislation we have on our statute books today, and which indeed has become an essential crutch for our economy, is due to the foresight, planning and courage of Mackenzie King and the Liberal government of that day.

In the light of the challenges with which our national economy, our international trade and our national security are being presented today, it was disconcerting to note the complacency with which the Minister of Finance basked in the very partisan applause of government members as he brought down his budget-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will answer questions after I have finished what I have to say. It was actually frightening to witness the minister's coyest and toothiest smile as he announced, after bringing down repeated record deficits, that this Conservative party, which in 1957 claimed to have the answer to all the problems, had finally given birth to a microscopic surplus of $12 million. This is true if, of course, you do not count the $210 million in total cash deficits which the government will have to borrow during the current year.
So, Mr. Speaker, a toothy smile and a debatable forecast of a $12 million surplus are the only assets which our Minister of Finance, with the excitement, the pride and the naivete of a nouveau riche, has to offer as a solution to the ever challenging economic, social, trade and security problems facing the country. Not only is this year's budget indicative of the government's alarming indecision and lack of plan and foresight in all fields, but once again the government has used the propaganda gimmick-in this case a nominal or fictitious surplus-in order to camouflage the true insignificance of the budget and its complete inadequacy to meet the real problems facing the government.
This time it is the Canadian people who must foot the bill for this latest Conservative

The Budget-Mr. Cardin publicity stunt, because the surplus was obtained at the expense of the 800,000 unemployed who were ignored in the budget and to whom nothing was offered, not even words of encouragement that a solution would be found to the very real and pressing unemployment emergency.
This surplus was obtained also at the expense of the provinces and municipalities who are still waiting for the equitable share of taxes promised to them three years ago. The two thirds of the civil service which was ignored in the budget and which had every right to claim an increase in salary also contributed to the Conservative propaganda surplus. So did the farmers, to whom so much had been promised by the Conservatives. Their net revenue dropped 7 per cent in 1959, yet the government proposes to do nothing about it.
We may ask, by shirking these real problems and responsibilities has the government effectively cut down its expenditures? No, Mr. Speaker; government expenditures this year will be $173 million more than they were last year. Because the Conservative policy of promising more than the country could afford, and because of the extremely high interest rates on our national debt, for which the government is responsible, the government is now caught in a vicious financial circle which apparently leaves no room for the consideration or solution of the fundamental problems that are now challenging our economy.
I was literally shocked to hear the minister say, as recorded at page 2671 of Hansard:
Our people have demanded social security, services and facilities from all levels of government on an expanding scale.
He says, "our people have demanded". Why, Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives not only claimed that this expanded social security was financially possible, they actually promised it in 1957. Not only did they promise it, they also promised to reduce taxes by $500 million as well. I submit that it is the height of arrogance, the height of effrontery for the Minister of Finance, after having blamed the previous Liberal government and the Bank of Canada for the present financial impasse, to attempt now to lay the blame on the people of Canada who had no reason to suppose that the Conservative promises were not only empty and irresponsible but, indeed, economically dangerous. Surely the Minister of Finance and the Conservative party must have realized these dangers.
If the government have no solution to the problems before us, at least they should have the decency to recognize and accept responsibility for their own mistakes without trying


to lay the blame anywhere and everywhere except where the blame really belongs.
How insignificant, Mr. Speaker, is the $12 million surplus compared to the $2.3 billion deficit the government has incurred over the past three years without being able to point to any real solution to any of the problems that now face us, and when in fact the increased payments in social benefits have been swallowed up and neutralized by high taxes, high interest rates and the high cost of living. How shallow and empty are the minister's words of confidence and smiles of self-satisfaction compared to the gravity and urgency of the real economic problems which he left out of his speech. The minister did not mention in his speech that the best economists in the country are agreed that the so-called Conservative prosperity, with its alarmingly high rate of unemployment, will cease and we will have at the end of 1960 the depression that the Conservatives prophesied under the Liberal regime.
How will the government, which has no financial reserves whatsoever, which has increased the national debt by $2.3 billion in three years, and which has burdened the economy for many years with an extremely high interest rate, be able to meet the financial obligations of a depression? How will the government, which in a period of so-called prosperity has seen its unemployment insurance fund decline from $874,574,000, in 1957 to $408,145,000 in February, 1960 be able to cope with the catastrophic number of unemployed which is characterized of a period of depression?
What is the government going to do about the continually increasing international payments deficit which rose this year to an unprecedented $1.5 billion? What confidence can Canadians have in a government which spent $5,607 million on our national defence last year and intends to spend this year $5,880 million, when we know that our national security seems to be centred around a useless Bomarc which the United States has discarded, and our obsolete CF-lOO's? The government apparently has no plans whatsoever for providing Canada with alternative adequate defence equipment, in spite of the fact that Canada's geographic position makes her a likely theatre for a third world war. Not only does the government not have a policy but it apparently refuses to discuss defence policy in this house or in committees set up for this purpose.
These are the facts, Mr. Speaker, which make the minister's $12 million surplus utterly ridiculous and insignificant, and which prove clearly that the government is not up to the responsibilities the people con-

ferred upon it in 1957. Not only is the government lacking in foresight, in planning and in leadership; it is also lacking in courage to face up to the problems and inform the public of the seriousness and the urgency of finding solutions to problems which now threaten Canada's economy and security. The government apparently still prefers to hide behind smiles and verbiage to save its face, but in doing so it is jeopardizing the true welfare of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier stated that the twentieth century would belong to Canada, he did not say there would be no problems and no challenges in our path. He took it for granted that these problems and challenges would be faced squarely and fearlessly. However, in making his prediction I am afraid Sir Wilfrid Laurier had not counted on Conservative indecision and maladministration.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words must be of congratulation to the Minister of Finance for his budget and its presentation. The fact that the Minister of Finance was able to introduce a balanced
The Budget-Mr. Phillips budget despite increased expenditures and without tax increases is, I think, a credit to his ability as minister. Most of the editorial comment has been very favourable, and I think the average Canadian is agreeably surprised that the budget is being balanced without tax increases.
Now a word on the subamendment which will be voted on this afternoon. I would refer specifically to the self-liquidating investment fund. I checked with the Oxford dictionary, and I found that the word "liquidating" when applied to business usually refers to bankruptcy. I think the subamendment can aptly be described as bankrupt.
While the minister has received a great many compliments, perhaps he would appreciate a suggestion along with the compliments he has received. I refer particularly to the reduced expenditures of the Department of Public Works. I have a number of projects in my constituency which, while not deleted, have unfortunately been delayed. I know the policy of reducing public works expenditures when a budget is being balanced; it is not new. Past ministers of finance have usually reduced public works expenditures too, but I wonder if in the long run this does not cost us more. Quite often there are emergency repairs and emergency dredging in various harbours which have to be carried out, and I think it increases the total cost of these projects.
The tariff changes are most welcome, and I think will be very beneficial to the textile industry in particular. Last year the potato growers received additional protection, protection which had been requested for years from the previous government. This year they have received greater protection. The tariff on processed potatoes entering this country will help that industry here, which is only in its infancy in Canada. During the present session of the Prince Edward Island legislature there has been considerable discussion over the efforts of the Prince Edward Island government to establish in that province a processing plant for potatoes. I am sure the tariff protection provided in this field will give them an extra incentive to bring their efforts to a successful conclusion.
In discussing the economy of the Atlantic provinces I had hoped to compare the percentage of the population with the gross national product, but I find there is no breakdown by areas.
Our primary industries are those associated with agriculture and fisheries, and perhaps a word on these two subjects might be appropriate at this time. Agriculture in the Atlantic provinces enjoyed a very good year

The Budget-Mr. Phillips in 1959. Our net farm income in Prince Edward Island will be almost identical with that for the year 1958, which was the second best year on record. Fishermen on the Atlantic coast enjoyed their best year in history in 1959. Total fish landings were worth $60 million for the year; and when we consider the employment that is provided in processing plants, the total value of the Atlantic fisheries is obviously far greater than the landed value. Our fisheries in Prince Edward Island are, of course, much smaller than those of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, but we had a record landing amounting to $4.2 million.
It is interesting to note the increase which has taken place in landings over the past decade. In 1949 the landed value in Prince Edward Island was $2.1 million. In 1959 it was $4.2 million, an increase of over 100 per cent in the decade. I may say that the greatest increase has occurred in the last few years and is partly due to increased prices received for the fish, especially by the lobster fishermen. It is also due to the efforts of the Department of Fisheries to modernize and improve fishing methods. More long-liners and draggers are being used, and the Department of Fisheries through the subsidy on these vessels and the loans provided by the provincial loans board is continuing to assist in the expansion of this industry.
During the present session we have heard a great deal about unemployment but very little about employment. During the past year employment in Prince Edward Island was at a record level. We had more people working last year than at any time in our history. This is probably due to the number of federal projects being carried out in the province, including the expansion of the R.C.A.F. station at Summerside, the Charlottetown airport, roads to resources, and public works.
While our employment has been high, wages unfortunately have not been high. In 1956 the average wage in Canada was $64.44. In Prince Edward Island it was only $47.50, and in Nova Scotia $52.90. In New Brunswick it was $55.10. In 1959 the average wage was $73.47. In Prince Edward Island it was $54.75; in Nova Scotia, $60.17 and in New Brunswick $60.39 per week. If we are to improve the economy of the Atlantic provinces and establish industries it is essential that we should increase our basic weekly wage. There is a tendency for the low wage rates in the maritimes to become perpetuated in a number of ways. The average wage in respect of federal contracts is considerably lower than in the rest of Canada. In the past winter I received complaints that the C.N.R. was paying 70 cents an hour for labour used to shovel


snow. I think hon. members will agree that this situation is extremely bad, and that efforts must be made to correct it.
There is in the maritime provinces today new interest and a feeling of encouragement over the results of a number of actions taken by this government. These actions include the adjustment grants given to the Atlantic provinces. The grants have been the greatest morale boost to the maritimes since confederation. We have also received assistance to establish thermal power plants, and we have received other forms of help which have laid the foundation for an improved future. I think the time has now come to act and build upon that foundation.
Our two main difficulties are lack of industry and transportation problems. In the past, under the Liberal government, industry in the maritime provinces-and the maritime provinces in general-was neglected. The former government had a policy of giving us a one-way ticket out of the maritimes, and it was aided in that regard by the genius of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who was very much in agreement with that policy.
In order to develop new industry in the maritime provinces we must have funds, and I suggest the establishment of a federal-provincial development fund for the maritime provinces. This fund could be used to extend our present industries and also to establish new industries, preferably in conjunction with our primary products of the farm and sea. The interest rate should be low enough to attract firms to the maritime provinces, and certainly it should not be above the rate charged on farm loans at the present time.
I	think this should be a joint fund of the dominion and provincial governments, and I hold this view for several reasons. First of all, maritimers themselves have a responsibility for improving their lot. We should play our part. Second, the provincial governments themselves have various plans for the establishment of industry. New Brunswick and Nova Scotia have already done a great deal to establish industries in their provinces, and the new government of Prince Edward Island has plans along the same lines. We should take advantage of their experience and of the experience and advice of the APEC.
Third, in the maritime provinces there is a suspicion of advice and direction from Ottawa. We dislike the idea of some official taking a two-day expedition to the Atlantic provinces and then returning as an authority on our problems and giving advice to the government. In fact, if I may refer to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate again, I would say that he is a classic example of the type of

individual who causes suspicion in the maritime provinces. He comes down for a couple of days at election time, and then returns and grows wheat on his farm in Rockcliffe.
A second method of developing industry in the maritime provinces would be through more consideration by and contacts with the Department of Defence Production. The present minister has gone a long way toward correcting several unfair situations that occurred under the former administration, notably that of the grouping of tenders. Formerly a number of tenders were called' together, and there was always at least one product with respect to which the maritime firms could not compete. This grouping has been largely eliminated, and its elimination has benefited us to a great extent in the Atlantic provinces. However, I should like consideration given to the United States plan of giving preference to depressed areas; where there is a labour surplus in one area, of giving a certain preference to the tender from that area.
I think we could also break up the tendency of having goods delivered to a central warehouse in Ontario. A couple of years ago a maritime firm tendered on a contract for army boots. The tender of the maritime firm was 9 cents a pair higher than that of a firm in central Canada, but they were required to deliver the boots to a warehouse in Ontario and they lost the contract. But when the boots were delivered to the warehouse in Ontario the army promptly shipped a large portion of them back to Camp Gagetown. If the maritime firm had been allowed to deliver those boots to Camp Gagetown they could have tendered' successfully.
Our second problem is transportation. It is not a new problem by any means. It has been plaguing us since confederation, and has increased considerably since world war II. Last year in the house I suggested that the Department of Transport give consideration to the establishment of a sea-train service. The department has taken notice of this suggestion and has given some consideration to it. But in the meantime I wonder whether we are not moving a bit too slowly in this regard. The United States is taking quite seriously sea-train, container service, or "fish-back", or whatever you care to call it. At the present time 17 vessels are under construction in the United States for this service.
I refer to an article in the Globe and Mail of May 20, 1959, which quotes an official of Grace Lines Incorporated as predicting that in the next 15 years the majority of general cargo ships will be of the container type, that 79951-0-193
The Budget-Mr. Phillips is to say they will be ships that take general cargo aboard in large vans, in which it is trucked directly from the shipside to the consignee. An article in the Duluth-Minnesota News Tribune of October 15, 1959 states that the interstate commerce commission has authorized "fish-back" container service from Duluth to Detroit and Cleveland. I feel that this type of service could be adapted from the maritimes to the ports on the seaway, and that the ports of Halifax and Saint John could be utilized on a year-round basis. This service could also be utilized for the shipment of products to the developed areas in northern Quebec and Labrador. The products could be placed in the container vans, shipped to Seven Islands and on by rail from this area.
We in the maritimes are greatly interested in the royal commission that is at present studying the transportation problem. However, we have a suspicion that transportation commissions tend to rehash what other commissions have gone over. When you consider the briefs that are submitted to these commissions you find that they are similar to previous briefs, and that each report of a royal commission on transportation seems to devote a good deal of space to reference to previous reports. If we looked around for different methods I think perhaps we could accomplish more than by attempting to doctor up our present methods of transportation.

Before one o'clock I was discussing the transportation problems of the maritime provinces. No discussion of our problems would be complete without reference to the three C's, namely the Prince Edward Island causeway, the Chignecto canal and the corridor road across Maine. These matters are now under study, and it is difficult to say too much until the studies are completed.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) has told me that an interim report on the causeway will be available shortly. I will make no further comment other than to say I hope we do not have too many interim reports and that a decision will soon be reached on this vital project. If for any reason a causeway is not feasible, then we must have plans approved immediately for the construction of a new rail carrying ferry for the Borden-Cape Tormentine route. I am naturally more interested in a causeway than in the other two projects but the Chignecto canal has taken on new importance with the announcement that there is a possibility of increased industry in the area if a canal is constructed.
There is a tendency to look upon these projects as a means of providing temporary employment in the maritimes. I think this attitude is entirely wrong. These projects should be looked at as part of the general development of the maritimes. If we are able to establish industry, improve our transportation problems, keep our young people at home, raise the population of the maritimes by a minimum of half a million people, we will have solved an awful lot of our difficulties; we will have a local market for our manufacturing and primary producers.
Recently I received a copy of the budget address delivered in the Prince Edward Island legislature. One part of that address should be very interesting to members of this house. It is the statement that 56 per cent of Prince Edward Island's revenues are obtained through grants from the federal government. We could only have achieved this large percentage of grants through the efforts of our present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and our able Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). We look forward with confidence to the next full scale dominion-provincial fiscal conference, and we are sure our problems will receive the same sympathetic consideration then as they received in 1957.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the occasion of the budget debate is the second and the last opportunity of hon. members to speak in general terms on the policies, general and financial, of the government and, within certain limitations, to speak on matters affecting their own constituencies, their own provinces and the country; also, on international affairs and relationships.
It is not my intention as I rise to speak in the budget debate to criticize the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) because he has brought in what might be called an interim budget, nor to criticize him, as has been done by some people and by editorial writers and suggest that he is waiting to introduce a budget of a more beneficial nature to the majority of the people of Canada just prior to an election. To me that is not an important piece of criticism because it is the general policy of governments and of election expediency to follow that procedure.
It may be a number of years before a change is made and a budget is introduced on the understanding that its underlying principle is the welfare of the country and not election expediency. However, in applying myself to the budget speech made by the Minister of Finance I personally can come to only one conclusion, namely that the principal motivating idea behind the remarks of the Minister of Finance the other day was that it is good policy to leave a few things unsaid. On analysis I do not think the budget speech of the Minister of Finance can be interpreted in any other way than that he considers it good policy to leave a few things unsaid.
This afternoon I want to speak on some of the things which the minister left unsaid. I can find no better way to introduce my remarks than to draw to the attention of hon. members the fact that in previous sessions, and even in the present session, I have made the statement that Conservatives and liberals, in government and out, supporting a free enterprise system as they do, stand completely indicted because the record of Canada conclusively proves that the only time we have anywhere near full employment in Canada is in time of war when men and women offer their lives for their country and goods are produced for destruction. But when men and women of Canada want to live for their country, to produce for consumption in a useful manner, then we reach the position where we find ourselves in a period of depression, recession and unemployment, as at the present time.
As I have already informed you, Mr. Speaker, I have made this statement once in the present session and previously in other

sessions, and I have been sneered at and jeered at from the government side because I said it. So, how better can I introduce my remarks in the budget debate this afternoon than to ask those who sit on the government side of the house this question? If they will not listen to an analysis by the group of eight in this corner of the house, will they pay any attention to an analysis made by one of their own members? I refer, of course, to the speech made on April 6 by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). It was quite remarkable how quiet Conservative members were when he made this statement, as found at page 2966 of Hansard:
For over 30 years I have sat here and listened to vigorous debates on the unemployment problem, only to see it temporarily relieved from time to time by the grim necessities of wartime. That is not good enough and I do not believe we have to endure it.
That was the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe speaking. If the treasury benches and Conservative members generally do not want to listen to us who have been saying the same thing for so many years, will they listen to what was said by one of their own members who, according to his own statement, has now heard one third of all the budgets ever delivered in the House of Commons of Canada? It is because of what he tried to say that I want to make my views known in the budget debate.
I not only listened to the Minister of Finance when he delivered his budget speech on Thursday night last week but I have read twice everything he said on that occasion and I want to say in unequivocal terms that the Minister of Finance in his presentation let the people of Canada down because of his refusal to face the facts and realities as they exist in our country. I was, as I think everybody else was, happy to hear him say that Canada is prosperous and booming but for the Minister of Finance of Canada to stand up in his place and ignore completely, with the exception of two sentences, the situation of the low income groups and the unemployed is a dereliction of responsibility on the part of the Minister of Finance.

speechtext:
You cannot tell me that there is a boom in Nova Scotia. No, there are grave and great troubles down there. Was there any mention in the speech of the Minister of Finance as to how that kind of problem
3056	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Winch is going to be handled? Was there any mention of the fact that when Avro took over Dosco they promised that coal mines would be open, not closed, but now there are fewer coal mines than there were before? When Avro took over Dosco citizens of Nova Scotia were turning out axles for railway freight cars. Now that is no longer being done in Nova Scotia because of Avro direction and control outside of Canada. The axles are coming from overseas. Are there any plans with respect to coal mining, with respect to the machining of parts that were previously made in Canada? Are there any plans for the 700 unemployed in Springhill?
Let us go to the other side of the country, to British Columbia. At the invitation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines I had the opportunity to travel home on a jet plane about two weeks ago. What is the situation there? According to the government's own figures, there are over 80,000 unemployed in British Columbia and the Yukon. In the construction industry alone there are over 12,000 unemployed. In the budget speech was there any mention of methods or plans by which these problems could be dealt with? No. There are just two sentences to the effect that things are not going right. In other words, we find that the policy speech of the Minister of Finance is one of wishful thinking, one of drift and absolute refusal to face up to the realities of the situation; a refusal to do any planning on behalf of those who are not prosperous.
What is the policy of the government with regard to planning for stopping the loss of industries and keeping people employed? There is none. In British Columbia during the past six months the whaling industry has been nonexistent, and this is the first time that has happened in 10 years. It is a small industry I admit, but it does mean an amount of $600,000 in annual payroll and it has meant several hundred thousands of dollars also to those who supply services such as petroleum companies, shipyards, vessel outfitters and so on. There has been no indication during this entire session, let alone in this budget speech, of any plans to maintain the herring industry of British Columbia, the whaling industry of British Columbia, the coal industry of British Columbia. Only lately the last coal mine closed down. There has not been a word about this situation. There has been no suggestion that would bring help to the closed coal mines of Nova Scotia or replace the loss of machine work since Avro bought Dosco. Now, as a result of outside control, products are shipped into Canada which we previously brought into being ourselves.


There may be good reasons for all these things. Surely, however, there is a good reason for asking the Minister of Finance and the government, have you given any thought to what is taking place? Have you any plans to ensure that industry is maintained? When some coal mines are in trouble, you have subventions. When the gold mines are in trouble, you have the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. When certain farmers need help, you come through to some extent. What we are asking is whether or not you have an over-all plan for the economy of Canada? I have never seen you help the farmers of British Columbia or the fishing industry of British Columbia or the coal mines of British Columbia. There are difficulties there, but there has been no mention of any of these problems in the minister's speech. I am saying that this government, because it is on a midterm basis, is doing nothing to try to resolve the problems of our country. I quite understand why you want a balanced budget. I maintain it is possible to have a balanced budget, if that is the criterion of success on the Conservative side, if you will take care of the problems which you have up until now ignored and make savings where you have refused to make them.
I know the logical question that one could ask at this point is: Where can you save money to take care of the planning for the depressed people and the depressed areas? I want to say that I, personally, and we in this group believe it is possible for a great deal of money to be saved in the Department of National Defence without any radical change in policy. Numerous statements from cabinet benches have made it clear already this session that the government's defence policy entails Canada being bound to NATO and NORAD. This, of necessity, means that Canada maintain a very close military and scientific relationship with the United Kingdom and the United States.
Canada now buys much of her military equipment from the United States, just as we used to buy it from the United Kingdom. In my opinion, therefore, it is not logical that we should be spending so much money on our defence research board when the same investigations and the same studies are being made by our allies in the United States and in the United Kingdom. I cannot understand why Canada should be doing the specialized research which is being done in other countries with whom we are so closely related.
I must be even more specific because if I say something should be done about planning and assistance for the unemployed and

low income groups and the depressed areas, then of course I must show where the savings can be made. I find it difficult to understand why Canada should develop its own Heller anti-tank rocket launchers; why we should be spending money to develop a solid fuel for missiles when Canada has no missiles. I should like to know why in our present estimates we are asked to spend so much money on research, design and development which has already been undertaken and, in some cases, concluded in the United States and the United Kingdom. I would ask the Minister of Finance, through you, sir, or perhaps the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) why we are wasting so much money on what he terms "unification".
Two years ago the estimates committee made a recommendation on unification to the Minister of National Defence, related to the medical and religious branches. This year we have been told unification has been completed. I have made a study of the answers and information from the Department of National Defence on this subject, and what do I find? I find that in the unification of the medical and chaplain corps the government seemed determined it would do its best to make no savings whatever for the taxpayers of Canada. In so far as the chaplain corps is concerned, the establishment was 273 before unification and it is still 273 after unification. Of course, there is one difference. Two junior ranks were removed but two new brigadier chaplains were appointed at headquarters in Ottawa. In the medical corps at unification we found that the number of medical officers was reduced from 477 to 472; but at the same time headquarters was padded by two additional lieutenant colonels. The result was that under government policy unification costs more than it did before.
I am convinced that if the Minister of Finance and the government believes in economy and efficiency it is possible to save millions of dollars, not only by a proper unification of the medical and chaplain corps but by the unification of all the armed services. This would make available the money which we say should be available under a balanced budget to help old age pensioners, veterans and the disabled, and in particular-I emphasize this-to take care of distressed areas and do some real planning. This has been completely ignored by this government and is emphasized by ignorance, incompetence and impotence in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance.
These points I have mentioned regarding planning policy are not the only matters left out of the speech the Minister of Finance made the other night. I know I speak on behalf of our group when I say that I feel
The Budget-Mr. Winch the minister, irrespective of the time he took, did not give any indication that he was taking the people in general and this House of Commons in particular into his confidence as to problems of the present and the future. I know, it is not too difficult for one to raise a little bit of Cain about the present, but my major worry is that there was nothing said about the future, except the wishful thinking that we are going into a time of prosperity and boom, which is denied by actual facts.
I would note from the remarks of the Minister of Finance that because of the way he is balancing the budget now the federal government will not have to go on a major borrowing spree this year. That will enable the provinces and the municipalities to have a more open door on borrowings than they have had in the past. I should like to ask if the Minister of Finance and the government have given any real thought to this problem of dominion, provincial and municipal governments having to go into the borrowing market. I should like to ask whether any consideration has been given to a new policy. I present this as my personal belief, but I do not think that our confederation in Canada is so parochial or provincial that it is not possible for the federal government and the provincial governments to get together on their borrowings, thereby reaching an understanding of the situation in the borrowers' market. Already I notice the Minister of Finance shakes his head and scowls.
Is there any difference between our nationalism in Canada and that in the commonwealth of Australia? In Australia every year the prime minister of the commonwealth and the premiers of the states get together and discuss their borrowing needs, reach an agreement, and then the federal government borrows all the money for the commonwealth and states by unanimous consent. That means a great deal. Then the federal government having borrowed all the money gives to each state the amount of money it requires at the same rate of interest as it had to pay. Then if the commonwealth government has a surplus, it loans the money to the states, which we call the provinces.
I spoke to ministers in five of the states of Australia. I spoke to one of the ministers of the commonwealth and he said it had been a wonderful system. There is just one borrowing by the commonwealth government on behalf of all states. I should like to suggest that this be considered by the minister. Is it impossible to believe that we cannot do a co-operative job in Canada on the same basis? I merely offer that as a suggestion.
My time is getting short, but I should like to say that the question of taxation is a

The Budget-Mr. Winch serious one to governments and to the people. The question of income tax and corporation tax is serious, as is also the question of plugging the loopholes. I do not go for all they do in the United States, but I do agree with the committee they have set up comprised of both houses which discusses matters of financial policy, does research and makes recommendations. I have been most interested to note that in the past 12 months in the United States very serious consideration has been given by the joint committee on internal revenue taxation and house committees on ways and means to try to arrive at a basis of income tax and capital gains tax to remove all loopholes, to give equity to everyone and to see that government receives its proper and fair return on the income of all people from the lowest standard of living to the highest.
I want to say that my reading of the work of those two committees in the United States leads me to believe that they are facing up to the facts and realities of taxation. I should like to suggest to the Minister of Finance that instead of things being done behind closed doors he place greater responsibility on committees of the House of Commons, on the Senate or on joint committees; that they should be able to conduct research on matters of taxation in order to see whether we, too, cannot come up with recommendations which will make our taxation laws less complicated, less iniquitous and will plug the loopholes.
I am led to believe that they think they can find the answer in the United States where the laws are somewhat different from ours. I do believe that the same principle if applied here under the leadership of the minister would mean a great deal to unity and understanding. What I think is required is a new taxation policy for Canada with regard to income tax and corporation tax. We have not yet a capital gains tax which I think is required if we are to have taxation according to ability to pay.
I notice that my time is almost up. May I conclude with these few words? Perhaps the minister and the government do not think that many of the proposals which we put forward are possible or conceivable. May I say that impossible things are simply those which have never yet been done. I state that with understanding, sincerity, knowledge and diligence the minister should go beyond his budget speech and endeavour to do things which we think are not impossible and not improbable, but inevitable in the interests of all the people of this country.
