subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Benidickson.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I wish initially to state that I intend to be brief, and I shall certainly make another reference to brevity in speaking in the house before I am finished.
Like others, I am justly proud of the budget presented in this house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). It is, I believe, a statement of true fact that the minister is the most capable minister of finance that this
The Budget-Mr. Winkler parliament has ever had. I know that he is accepted as such in financial circles, and even the minister's critics across this country will in due course appreciate his tremendous abilities in his present position, and I know it will be evident in the management of the affairs of this country.
To support my belief it is not necessary for me to search far following the presentation of the budget. Indeed, many of the headlines back up what I have just indicated. They also support the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) when some of the headlines forecast "more cash jingles in Canadian pockets." Then, we have the word "courageous" and other such headlines. I would add to that just plain common sense. This, of course, is in direct opposition to what the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) thought.
Then, further, a few days following the budget, we also noticed that the headlines were running a little more in the right direction. We know that defence costs are declining and that the cost of living index has declined for the fourth straight month.
I do not doubt that less complimentary headlines could be found; but I am one of those- and I know anyone who has read the statistics involved in the presentation of the budget knows it full well-who believes that the compliments I have referred to are well founded.
There is good reason for confidence in this year's business as a result of the minister's forecast. Even in the light of the fact that many of the expenditures which he indicated in his white paper were considerably higher than the year previous, even with the decline in the deficit-and I am sure that the trend will continue-to mention but a few of those to indicate how the government has acted and how the minister's forecasts have worked out in regard to expenditures, I would like first of all to refer to the expenditures for agriculture. I will not make these comparisons throughout but they are all figures obtained from the white paper presented by ministers of finance and mostly, of course, by the present minister.
In 1956-57 the previous government spent $5,019,000 on supports; in 1957-58 it was $5,988,000; in 1958-59 it was $15 million; and in 1959-60, $57,700,000 was spent in support of agriculture. To assure the leader of the C.C.F. party that the door is open at all times I think the trend indicated here would support that thinking. I know from my own experience with the minister, and certainly with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hark-ness) that such has been the case. After all, the expenditures that were made on behalf

The Budget-Mr. Winkler of my constituents in regard to compensation for rabies which was not an inconsiderable amount of money.
Then, we move on to university grants, provincial subsidies, tax-sharing arrangements, farm supports, health grants, hospital insurance, veterans' affairs and a great host of others. These expenditures have increased. I think we can assure the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) that the veterans' welfare will also be looked after, as well as all other phases of our social program.
As announced by the minister, this government has now substantially removed itself from the money market. It might be wise to comment on what the results can be and will be. It is now becoming quite evident that the interest rates are dropping and the inevitable benefit will redound to every level of government in its capital spending. Also there will be a tremendous benefit to industry and I would expect that our exchange position with the United States will improve in the immediate future. I think the indications are that way now. This, of course, will be most desirable on the part of industry.
What about the projected surplus? This morning we heard again about how small it was, how insignificant it was and so on. The opposition have tried to point out that the trend is maybe one of wishful thinking rather than planning. Although in my own estimation the percentage to the total budget may be small, yet the trend is correct and we can be justly proud of the minister's efforts. As a matter of fact, it would not surprise me if at the end of the current fiscal year the surplus was about 10 times as great as he forecast.
The minister and the government have made one point very clear in financial matters, namely that they did not adopt the attitudes of the previous government by suggesting to the Canadian citizens that they cannot look after their own affairs. They have spent the money in the interests of Canadians and of the entire economy. They did not, as one hon. member mentioned this morning, take $50 million and stick it here and another $50 million and hide it there and another $165 million and hide it some place else. We are spending the money that we take in in taxation on the citizens, in their interests and in the interests of Canada. I am sure that as the forecast of this budget indicates the minister will go on to repair all of the damage that has been done in the past and that we shall have a very sound economy again in the very near future.
The opposition critic was very generous in giving credit to the minister on two points, as reported at page 2863 of Hansard. But, of course, what most amazed everyone is the


fact that he could not complete the 20-minute period that was left to him on budget night. With all deference, I think that mere conformity to tradition would lose him a tremendous number of points in anybody's view. We are all concerned with any of the situations that are brought home to us but it has been evident in this debate that the members of the Liberal party have been very hard pressed to find any criticism that is sound; indeed, the entire party, not only the critics, have been dashed in their hopes of a much higher deficit, with increased taxation, in the budget. I think this is very evident, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to join with the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) who stated that Canada has been most fortunate in that most of the members of parliament who have held the position of minister of finance have been of good sound character, have been good citizens, and so on. This is indeed true, and it is most certainly true of my predecessor who was also the predecessor of the minister now in office. I note, however, Mr. Speaker, that this gentleman is making public statements similar to those of his party members and I should like to quote from the Owen Sound Sun-Times of March, 1960. I regret I have not the date, but I have the clipping before me. It says:
Harris says deficit may be $600 million.
This is an indication that they were all hoping to enjoy something like that, a little more doom, a little more gloom. We know now this was wishful thinking, but Mr. Harris went on to say that the:
-deficit will come as a shock to the Conservatives unless they can find some money pretty fast.
They were going to be embarrassed. It seems to me that he, like other members of the Liberal party, would do anything in his power to make the Canadian picture and the Canadian scene bad. They are prognosticators of nothing but ill for Canadian citizens. We must conclude that they would stop at absolutely nothing to regain power. It is a difficult thing for me to understand that Mr. Harris would be such a protagonist of the Liberal cause after the treatment accorded to him by his party supporters at the leadership convention in Toronto such a short time ago.
In making his criticism the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River stated that if he were in power he would consult the experts on what to do and then, of course, he would do something, he said. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members, what one very well qualified expert has to say. I refer to an article in a morning paper today reporting

a speech made in Vancouver on April 7. The article says that a prominent Montreal analyst said:
-Canada has suffered from very poor financial and fiscal policies. The Bank of Canada, he said, eased money in 1955 when other countries were tightening up on money.
"I don't think they should have," said Mr. Bolton. "It was an error which has hounded us ever since."
I do not think we have to go too much further to agree that this is the case and that the present situation in which we find ourselves is only emerging from all of those things with which we have had to deal.
I should like to refer for a moment to trade. Trade, of course, will play a most important part in the coming economic upswing. I know that the figures published for January and February show an increase of 27.1 per cent and there is no reason to believe that this upswing will alter. Indeed, although I have not been able to get a firm figure from the bureau of statistics, I have a statement here made by the Canadian association of purchasing agents that orders placed in the month of March are 27 per cent ahead of a year ago and in all industries reporting production is ahead by 33 per cent.
The minister has indicated that he is aware of the importance of imports and the impact they will have on our economy, and it cannot be other than good planning and salesmanship that the increase is of such great proportions. We all know what foreign imports, which are usually made in a much cheaper labour market, mean to us and we would not want the impact on our industries to be as great as has occurred in other countries. I note that the New York News of March 29 reports that many small businesses in the United States have been forced to close their doors and that even the big boys are feeling the pinch. Allow me for a moment, by making reference to that paper, to indicate the situation there. We note, for instance, that 12 years ago the United States, such a large country, imported only 1,500 foreign cars and at that time exported 261,000 cars. Last year they imported 668,000 and exported a new low of 117,000. So goes the whole picture. Four million radios were imported and exports were negligible by comparison.
Another important point I note is that one of the oldest sewing machine companies in the United States, established over 80 years ago, threw in the towel three years ago and now distributes only a foreign-made product. We do not want this sort of thing to happen in Canada, and I am sure that the ministers concerned will take the necessary action to see that this does not occur. We would also not want a socialistic atmosphere 79951-0-194
The Budget-Mr. Winkler to present itself because to live under such circumstances would create chaos. Let us not forget that after socialism comes the hammer and the sickle.
I believe that members of the opposition- apparently they do not like to listen to what I have to say-would rather engage in the sort of talk that breeds great lack of confidence and we know, of course, that their discourses are strictly for public consumption. I should like to say that on this particular point alone they are damaging to a great degree some of the possibilities that exist and by no stretch of the imagination are they contributing anything that would be constructive.
I should now like to make a few remarks regarding local industry in my constituency. I have mentioned before in the house that in the main it is furniture manufacturing and, as in other industries, we note a very rapid rise in the rate of imports of furniture. This is an industry that does not and has not had the good fortune of enjoying an export market. There is a possible market in the United States but the tariff and the export procedure make shipments almost impossible. We note that the sharpest increase in imports is from the United States, a market which, as I have said, it is difficult for us to enter. However, there is an alarming increase in imports from other countries in the world and it is necessary for me to mention this matter because if a situation arises in the future where things become impossible I will have to bring this matter to the attention of the government with much greater force.
I should like to refer to a report in the Montreal Gazette of April 7 of a speech in Montreal by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). The article is headed, "Join Free Trade Area, Martin Urges". I can only say that we in the constituency of Grey-Bruce know full well what this means now and we would be remiss if we did not remind the people of the country and the government that this is not the time to consider such a move. What would they have us do? Destroy secondary industry in this country? Allow the farming industry of the country to be torn to shreds by producers who can snow us under? We have heard enough of this already today. I congratulate the government on any move they make which will support local and domestic industry against unfair competition such as we are beginning to experience in our own way.
I might also mention that I live in an area which is very close to lake Huron and Georgian bay. It is a sad reflection for me

The Budget-Mr. Macnaughton to see the deterioration of our once great fishing industry in these waters. The participants in the industry are now almost all out of business due to the lack of fish.
A comprehensive picture was given in the house by my colleague, the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Noble), and I think it would be wise for the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) to investigate the possibility of planting fish that are known to thrive in such waters and are able to resist the eel and the smelt. Also, and I appreciate that this is primarily a matter of provincial concern, some action is necessary to stop the reinfestation of these waters from the sea. This is a program which I believe could be done very easily and at small expense. Inasmuch as funds are appropriated by the government for the support of the great lakes fisheries commission it would not be beyond the bounds of reasonable expectation for the minister and the department to give some consideration and leadership in this matter.
Finally, I should like to refer to the cost involved in speaking in the House of Commons. As was indicated previously this session, I believe it is in excess of $1,820 an hour. In consideration of the suggestions regarding economy-I hope I am being brief this afternoon in consideration of others who would like the floor-may I say that I am of the opinion that we should amend the rules of the house in some way to cut down the time that I feel is wasted. There may be some who think that I have wasted time today, but it is with that purpose in mind that I am speaking. I believe that a great waste of time is also brought about by people who are impressing their views upon the house and the country unnecessarily. I refer to the filibuster that we are experiencing these days. There are ways and means of putting one's feelings vehemently before the right authorities without wasting the time of the house and depriving hon. members of the opportunity to bring worth-while private resolutions and bills before the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) forecast a surplus for the fiscal year 1960, modest though it may be, all Canadians were pleased. The minister's determination to abandon deficit spending, which has been the feature of his last two budgets, is a step in the right direction, at least one step in setting the government's house in order. The deficit spending of the present government for the past two years has been causing grave concern to a great many Canadians who consider this policy a threat to our future economic prosperity. All the people who hold this view, and I list

myself amongst them, complain in particular that the country is not receiving the benefits which should have accrued from this deficit spending.
Experts are generally agreed that government spending of the nature and the scale of the past few years-I should say perhaps for the past three years-is not the most effective way of fighting a short recession. Such spending leaves in its wake many economic difficulties. The president of the Royal Bank, Mr. James Muir addressing the shareholders at their annual meeting on January 8, 1959, said:
Last year, as in previous recession years, and while the economy was still on the downgrade, I urged tax cuts by government and price cuts by business. Instead of tax cuts last year, which would have encouraged business activity while reducing pressure on prices, we got increased government spending. Instead of an immediate deficit last year, timed to coincide with the depth of the cycle, we find ourselves today with a delayed deficit which has timed itself to coincide with the present recovery and the emergence of a new inflationary potential. For it is the great disadvantage of government expenditures as a cure for recession and it is both ponderous and irreversible; it takes time to get projects under way, and once started they must be completed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman give the date of that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, certainly. The date of that was January 8, 1959, the report of the president of the Royal Bank to the shareholders.
In his statement on tax policy, which appears on page 2681 of Hansard of March 31, 1960, the Minister of Finance said:
As I said a year ago, and as I have repeated in this house and elsewhere on a number of subsequent occasions, sound tax policies must be flexible and adapted to changing economic conditions. The onset of the 1957 recession called for lower taxes, higher expenditures and heavier capital commitments in order to offset the downward trends in the private sector of the economy and the decline in the external demand for some of our basic products; and I put such proposals before the house in December, 1957 and again in June, 1958.
It strikes me as very strange indeed that the minister now acknowledges that lower taxes was one of the specific features of his program to deal with the recession in 195758. If memory serves me aright, I recall how vigorously the minister opposed and condemned, both on the hustings and in the house, the Liberal policy of tax reductions as a means of stimulating economic activity. I find it equally strange that the minister did not remind the members of this house that he withdrew a good part of the benefits of these tax reductions in the 1959 budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
However, that is all in the past. What about the future? In my opinion, the minister is taking a big gamble in forecasting a modest surplus. First, he is assuming that there will be no decline or hesitancy in the rate of our economic growth. Second, he is assuming that each department of government will rigidly control its expenditure. Third, he is assuming that our export trade will continue to grow.
With regard to the first assumption, the minister chooses to ignore some of the danger signals in our economy which suggest that the rate of growth may be slower than that which he predicted. He rejects the warnings of the leading economists in the government service, in the academic field and in business, for most economists, I think, agree that rough economic weather is ahead for late 1961 and 1962. An increasing number of economists fear that the first wind of the storm may come in the last quarter of 1960 and the beginning of 1961. In other words, our Canadian economy may be bucking strong winds during a good part of the last half of the 1960 fiscal year.
I do not intend to quote these authorities, as many of them have been cited in this debate so far by other members. However, I do want to point out to the house that a slowdown in our economic growth could easily turn the minister's modest surplus into a deficit and thus could force the government to borrow substantially more than the estimated amount of $210 million.
The minister's second assumption is equally risky. He is demanding departmental control of spending which does not allow even for a normal and expected degree of overspending. There is no margin for the unexpected necessary expenditure. While the minister is certainly to be congratulated for asking for strict control throughout government departments, I wonder if he is being realistic, considering the smallness of the surplus he anticipates?
Have we any hope that the minister may have suggested to his colleagues in the cabinet that we have reached a plateau with regard to government spending and that the various government departments must remain on this plateau for several years to come? I think we should all keep in mind that the basic problem is not only balancing the budget, but at what point or where do you balance the budget? There is no purpose in talking about a balanced budget if in each succeeding year the budget is balanced at fantastically higher and higher levels. This is, in effect, only kidding the people.
The minister's third assumption is, perhaps, his greatest gamble. Canada's export trade, for the past few years does not encourage 79951-0-194J
The Budget-Mr. Macnaughton many people to share the view of the minister or of his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill). Here, the two ministers seem to be in a dream world of their own. Perhaps the Minister of Finance has ventured there so his colleague will not be lonely. I will have more to say about trade shortly. At the moment I merely want to say that the Canadian exporter finds it increasingly difficult to get a fair share of the increase in overseas markets. The economic vitality of western Europe and the United Kingdom, the entry of Russia on a large scale as a large and vigorous trader, is producing a degree of competition in international trade unknown since the end of the second world war.
Our exporters find it harder to retain their traditional markets and harder to acquire new ones. A real increase in our export trade may be slower in the future than it has been in the past.
These are the gambles the minister is taking. As Canadians interested in the economic well-being of our country we wish the minister luck, though many of us feel he has balanced the budget with a hope and a prayer.
I have spoken of the favourable aspects of the budget. Now let me comment on some of the disappointments. The minister has announced no policy or program to deal with the serious deficit in our international accounts and the problems which our exporters are encountering in the international markets.
Surely the minister realizes that responsible government demands leadership. Three weeks ago the members of this house discussed international trade. We were told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that all was rosy in the garden. He failed to define government policy. Now the Minister of Finance has spoken and he has failed to state a policy or outline a program to ease our situation. This I find very strange indeed.
The minister is the one member of the government, apart from the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) who can direct and stimulate our economy by the policies he persuades his colleagues to adopt. Government departments and agencies can act effectively if the economic policy of the government is known.
The Bank of Canada, for example, can manage our monetary system and has done so brilliantly and successfully for many years; but the Bank of Canada cannot manage or direct our economy. That is the job of the government.
The deficit in our international account is serious. The minister himself acknowledges the fact. He urges us to work and save but

The Budget-Mr. Macnaughton does not tell us what he intends to do about it. His attitude appears to be the well known attitude of laissez faire.
What can be done about it? Are we importing too many consumer goods? If so, I suppose the importation of consumer goods could be controlled by a quota system. But a quota system is not acceptable to Canadians, and furthermore it would only antagonize our friends and customers. A quota system would invite retaliation and could lead to economic isolation. The problem of the deficit in our international accounts could be remedied to a degree by various government controls, such as government control of exchange and by the formation of a capital issues committee. But controls in any form are not acceptable to the Canadian people. The institution, and furthermore the administration of such controls would be complex. Experts also doubt that they would be as effective in application as they appear to be in theory, and I doubt if the advantages would outweigh the disadvantages.
The adoption of such controls would be contrary to the trend abroad where currencies have been freed and public and private investment encouraged. I believe such controls would lose us many friends and certainly as many customers. The minister has, quite rightly, rejected all these proposals, but what alternatives does he suggest? He certainly has not told us of any.
If we are going to import goods and capital at our present rate we must earn more abroad on the sale of Canadian goods. We must sell more in our traditional markets. We must find new markets for our traditional export products. We must encourage the export of new products in raw or semifinished form which are not now being exported in sufficient volume. We must seek new markets abroad for all our products, industrial as well as agricultural.
It is almost trite to say that competition has become an increasingly important factor in world trade, but how very true it is. Other countries are no longer forced to shop in the North American market as they were in the years immediately following the war. They can now purchase their goods from a number of suppliers. We are in a buyer's market, no longer a supplier's market. Our ability to export is no longer measured by our ability to supply foreign markets. Our productive capacity permits us to meet almost any foreseeable demand. Canada's ability to export today and even more so in the future will be measured by our ability to meet competition and our success in opening and developing new markets abroad.
Our new exports, uranium, iron ore, petroleum and now natural gas have helped


The Russian threat demands that our government recognize the possible consequences to this country and begin to take appropriate action which would include the immediate study of the long range effects of Soviet competition on Canada's export trade. Canadian exporters have every right to expect some guidance as to the nature of this threat. All we ask is that the government show a sense of urgency such as the situation warrants. Surely Canadians have a right to expect far more from their government than what has been done so far. A mere indication that the situation is being watched and that the government will protect our interests if necessary is not enough.
Canada's economic life blood is dependent upon the vigour of its foreign trade. This is Canada's historical position, as professor Hugh G. J. Aitken said in a seminar at Duke University in the summer of 1958 under the heading "The Changing Structure of the Canadian Economy". I should like to quote his words, because I think they are very significant-
Canada, from the beginning of its history, has been a vulnerable economy, exposed to pressures and stimuli from more advanced nations. Its development has been geared to external demands and external challenges.
This government has failed to appreciate this economic fact. It has failed to appreciate, too, that Canada needs a favourable international trading climate more than any other nation. That is why Canada must take the initiative in advancing plans for the basis of international trade.
We sometimes fail to realize the size of the markets being created by the regional trading blocs. Mr. John McCullough, a prominent United States chartered accountant, put out a private booklet on the financial implications of the common market. It was written for the public of the United States, but what he describes is applicable to Canada to an even greater extent. Mr. McCullough had this to say:
Many a corporate financial executive will decide in 1960 what his company is going to do about the vast new mass market now evolving in the common market countries of Europe. Among the factors impelling this decision are:
First, it is expected that the common market will evolve into a mass market of 170 million people by 1970 with a progressively increasing standard of living; that the gross national product of the common market countries will increase by then to $400 billion (ours was $442 billion in 1958) ;-
He is referring to the United States.
-and that there will be a tremendous increase in demand for consumer goods and concomitant capital goods. Substantial sums of European and American capital have been expended or are planned for expenditure on the basis of these expectations.

Then in paragraph No. 6 he says this:
Finally, corporate financial executives must consider the projected effect of foreign competition upon their United States business and their foreign business outside the common market. Development of know-how, increase in efficiency and improvement of economic position, superimposed on lower wage rates, has materially strengthened foreign competition in the United States domestic market. Already, some American manufacturers have not been able to meet this competition and there is reason to believe that others will suffer.
Other regional groups can be equally large. Unless Canada is aggressive and imaginative in its trading policies and particularly in its negotations with other countries, it could well be that we would be shut out and driven into economic isolation.
The situation demands a sense of urgency on the part of the government. It is my hope that the Minister of Finance whose responsibility it is to guide and direct our economy will initiate without delay a polcy to deal effectively with our deteriorating international position in trade and our deficit on international account.
Mr. Pallet!: In view of his last statement, will the hon. member answer a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should be glad to answer.
Mr. Pallet!: Has there not been a tremendous upsurge in January and February of this year?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think it is fair to take one or two months. You might as well say there is a tremendous upsurge of employment in the summer time. Of course there is, because of geographic and weather conditions. The same thing applies to trade. I could read the hon. member an article which was discussed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on a question of privilege. It appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press. I have it here but I will not waste time by reading it. I should like to finish as I have a few more minutes left. I should like to conclude my speech because I am sincere about the necessity of there being a sense of urgency on the part of the government to initiate, to undertake and to explain to the Canadian people, to do something about a trading policy which they have not had for the last three years and which has gradually crept up on us and will eventually destroy our position in the European market.
I am not alone in thinking this. Mr. John Meyer, the financial editor of the Montreal Gazette, on Monday, April 4, wrote as follows:
The budget would have given finance minister Fleming the opportunity to give direction to the economy had he recognized there was a need for direction. In standing pat on tax levels, he also
The Budget-Mr. Hicks
stood pat on the tired assumptions that everything will come out right in the end. That posture is not one which can much longer be afforded.
Then he concludes with this paragraph:
But surely the budget is not intended as a catalogue of the difficulties confronting action on this point. Rather, the difficulties should constitute the challenge. Mr. Fleming, unhappily, does not seem to be aware that the challenge has been offered.
I hope sincerely that the Minister of Finance will recognize this challenge of trade, deficit financing, the need to hold the line, the need to control expenditures except in those cases in which we decide in this house that they are socially necessary. I hope he will hold the line and accept this challenge that he give us a trade policy, a financial policy, and do something about the threat of Russian trade competition.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like very much to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming)	and also his	parliamentary
secretary (Mr. Bell) on the very fine budget brought down by them and on the way in which it was brought down. Of course, that is exactly what everybody expected would happen. It has been well received in the press and over the radio. In view of that fact I do not intend actually to discuss the budget very much. However, I want to read one article. I quote from the Ottawa Citizen of April 2, 1960 these words. This article may have been quoted by somebody else when I was not in the house. However, it is such a good article that it will not hurt one bit to quote it a second time. It is headed "U.S. Politician Praises Our Balanced Budget". I may say that this is the best authority in the United States on Canadian affairs. It reads as follows:
One of the most knowledgeable men in the U.S. congress on Canadian affairs Friday praised the Canadian budget for "resisting temptation to intervene artificially" with Canada's trade imbalance and the foreign premium on her dollar.
Representative Frank Coffin of Maine says that the budget required "a good, long respectful look northward" by this country's authorities.
He was speaking, of course, of United States of America.
"Although an increase in expenditures of about 3 per cent is contemplated, with defence, civil service pay raises and social security accounting for the increases, the forecast is for a balanced budget," Coffin said in a statement.
At the same time Canada expects to continue her remarkable growth rate of about 6 per cent, about twice that of the U.S. in recent years.
"The government has also set a good example for the U.S. in resisting temptation to intervene artificially to attack Canada's trade imbalance problem and the dollar premium problem, while responding more selectively to special problem areas such as textiles.
"All in all it should hearten us in the U.S. to know that Canada's outlook for the future is that of a growing economy playing a significant and responsible role in the world of trade."

The Budget-Mr. Hicks
Mr. Speaker, you will probably recall that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) was speaking in the debate on the speech from the throne he mentioned the establishment of a House of Commons committee to consider the rules under which parliament operates. I refer you to page 65 of Hansard of January 18. Later in the debate on the speech from the throne as reported at page 402 of Hansard the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith), having in mind similar ideas, gave seven or eight suggestions about changing the rules of the house. A proposal I should like to make is the installation of a projector by means of which a member could use slides or even a position where a good map could be hung in this House of Commons. I know that many hon. members would ask, where are you going to put a map in this house so that we can all see it? I think we could see it all right if it were up over that clock. Perhaps that would be a good place to put it now because time is a factor and I have quite a few things to say.
In fact I find myself at the moment in need of a large map of British Columbia as I wish to speak for a few minutes about three rivers. I refer not to the city between here and Quebec but to three great rivers of British Columbia, and I wish to point out the terrible flood danger of the lower Fraser river, as seen by me in 1948.
One of the rivers is in the southeastern section of the province; I refer to the Columbia river. The first river I wish to discuss is the Columbia river with about a third of its length in British Columbia. It rises in Columbia lake about 70 miles north of Cran-brook, British Columbia and north, of course, of the U.S. border in the Rocky mountain trench. It flows north to Golden, thence in a horse-shoe shape to which the Big Bend highway corresponds and back south. At the most northern end of the Big Bend is the Mica dam site, the largest storage site for power in the project. Then it goes south to Revelstoke and takes in the drainage waters of the Arrow lakes and also goes south and takes in the Kootenay lakes and river and other valleys and crosses the 49th parallel into the northeast portion of the state of Washington. Thence it flows south to Portland and flows into the ocean there. It flows in British Columbia a distance of 480 miles. Its flow is in total length 1,225 miles and the total fall is 2,655 feet. The total British Columbia basin is 29,500 square miles, and the total United States basin is 5i times that much, namely 219,500 square miles.
The Columbia river is one of the really great rivers of this continent, with its length and run-off only exceeded by the Mississippi


going south, by the Mackenzie going north and by the St. Lawrence going east. As we know, the power potential of this great river is enormous. As negotiations are under way at the moment among the United States, Canada and British Columbia I do not care to say more at the present time about the Columbia expept that we must avoid overflooding of valuable land in certain areas.
The Mica dam is the important dam to build from the Canadian and British Columbian point of view. This morning I received a resolution put out by the Revelstoke board of trade and I wish to read three sections of this resolution:
Whereas construction of Mica dam will provide large land reclamation areas in the Columbia basin as opposed to flooding resulting from construction of the high Arrow dam, and
Whereas construction of the high Arrow will delay commencement of Mica dam for a period of many years, and
Whereas Mica dam will provide British Columbia with an ample and lasting supply of low-cost public power and control of water,-
And so on. They are very much in favour of having the Mica dam built.
For a very brief moment I want to turn to the Peace river. This great river originates north of Prince George, almost in the centre of the province of British Columbia. The Parsnip flows north, and from the north the Finlay flows south to Finlay Forks, where it meets the Parsnip to start the Peace, which in turn flows east and crosses the British Columbia-Alberta border into Alberta and continues on in a northeasterly direction to enter into the Slave system. The source of the Peace is the home of the famous, or some people even call it the infamous, Wenner-Gren project.
The Peace River Power Development Company was incorporated in October, 1958. The company's proposed hydroelectric project for the generation of four million horsepower of electricity is situated at two proposed dam sites at Peace river canyon, 80 miles west of the British Columbia-Alberta border. It is planned that the proposed development of power will be in three parts.
First, present projects; there are two dams at the Peace river canyon, an ideal place for dams, near Portage mountain. The first dam is 600 feet high with a 7,000 foot crest. The second dam is a few miles further downstream and is 150 feet high with a 1,700 foot crest. The second project is two additional dams still in British Columbia, further down the river, and the third downstream dam is in Alberta along the Peace and the Slave rivers.
The unique feature of the project is the size of the reservoir lake which will be formed. It extends 70 miles above the canyon

and 200 miles in the rocky mountain trench. This huge lake will provide great storage capacity, more than the present storage of all hydro dams in British Columbia, as well as the three nearest in the United States. It is estimated that this lake 2,250 feet above sea level will take seven years to fill and by that time it will be able to develop 750,000 horsepower. The estimated cost is $700 million.
Storage in the reservoir is provided for 88 million acre feet of water, which is six times that of Grand Coulee dam. The 200 mile long reservoir lies in a northeasterly direction in the rocky mountain trench, with its southerly end about 63 miles north of Prince George or, in other words, it is something like 50 to 70 miles from the Fraser river. The average width of the reservoir is four miles and the area about 900 square miles.
The big objection to this project is the fact that the power is manufactured so far from where it will be required unless, of course, business and industry move to where the power is. It is 600 miles from there to Vancouver, where most of the power would be used under present conditions, and it goes by Prince George, Quesnel, Williams lake and follows the Fraser to Vancouver. There is also objection to the fact that so much arable land is being flooded.
The third objection is that there is very severe criticism of the handling of this project.
Having said this about the two great rivers, the Columbia and the Peace, I want to turn to the Fraser and to give hon. members some idea of what flooding has done in the past and show that things are not safe at the present. We certainly do not want to have a repetition of the 1948 flood.
The Fraser river is entirely within the province of British Columbia. The basin contains 90,000 square miles and that is about one quarter of the entire province of British Columbia. The area drained by the Fraser is all inside the great mountain system known as the American Cordillera.
The Fraser originates in the area around Yellowhead pass, or mount Robson, and after 70 miles in a northwesterly direction in the main trench it turns south from the trench at Prince George, where it is only about 60 miles from, as I said before, the storage reservoir of the Peace, and flows some 400 miles. At Lytton, the Thompson river enters the Fraser. It cuts through the coast range in a deep canyon, passes through Hell's Gate on to Hope, where it is then 100 miles from its mouth at Vancouver. From source to
The Budget-Mr. Hicks mouth it flows 850 miles. In the north it drains such lakes at Taka and Stuart and the Nachaka river, and further along, Quesnel, Chilcotin, Bridge River, Lillooet, Thompson and the lower Fraser valley are all drained by it. Over 70 per cent of the area of the basin lies above the 3,000 foot range, which is the limit for agricultural crops; hence, the importance of the fertile agricultural lands in the short lower Fraser valley area. The great flood danger lies in the last 80 miles of its course after it has passed through Hell's Gate and gone on down past Hope, about 20 miles.
On May 24, 1948 I was attending a Rotary convention in Bellingham, Washington, about 20 miles south of the border, and I felt rather uneasy, knowing that the water was coming up at Agassiz, where I was situated at that time. I decided I would go home the next morning. I got out and going down to see what was going on I saw the dikes. I found there a flow of about 10 feet deep, 20 feet wide, just gradually pouring in over the farm land and the people were beginning to move their cattle. The people were beginning to move out of the area. At the time I thought it was a terrible thing that this could happen. Actually, I felt that this might not be too bad at all because the water would come in gradually that way and it would not be a case of breaking the dike and chasing people out.
On that day the reeve of the municipality came to me and said, "You know quite a few people, employees or officials, of the Canadian Pacific Railway; I wish you could arrange to take charge of evacuating all the people out of the Agassiz valley except, of course, the people we want to work." I took charge of that work. We got a lot of the older people and the women and children out. It just so happened that the old hotel in Vancouver was vacant at that time and the Red Cross took over and looked after the people. A day or two after this the railroad washed out just west of Agassiz and we had to send more people out by Harrison lake down to Harrison river to a station further down and then on into Vancouver. A few days later the river burst through the C.P.R. right of way at Hatzic and the highway and as soon as this happened the water began to recede a little in the Agassiz area.
Shortly after I had been given a charge of evacuating people Premier Byron Johnson of British Columbia, came to me one day and asked me if I would take complete charge of all the work at Agassiz. My terms of reference were something like these: "You are in charge. Help the people. Anything you want to have done, initial it, pass it on and it will go. Do what you can to help

The Budget-Mr. Hicks all the people and save all the money you can without anyone getting hurt."
At that time we had moved cattle into a cemetery roughly two miles by one mile in size. There were 700 cattle there and approximately 100 people had their tents right among the graves. About the third day afterward, I believe, I went that way and I could hear the catle bawling a mile away. Feed had run out and I actually saw cattle there straddling shrubs as they went looking for food. They would straddle a shrub, pin the top down, and eat the leaves. That is how hungry the cattle were.
We at the experimental farm were a little more fortunate because the C.P.R. right of way had helped to hold the water back until it got by Agassiz. We had our office and our whole herd there and we were able to get clean water that ran down the mountain. It was a wonderful source of water supply for the people left there. I think that 17 people slept in our house one night.
I am telling you these things to place before you the importance of controlling flooding on the lower Fraser river. As the flood receded you can imagine the work that had to be done. Where the water had got inside houses it had raised floors and shoved sills out and when the houses dried out the sand left on the floor was as hard as cement. I want to pay a tribute to the provincial department of health. They inspected all the houses, wells and so on before people were allowed to go back to their homes again.
Agassiz is a cesspool town and the town, of course, was flooded. I actually saw fish going in the back door of the butcher shop and swimming out the front door and some of the ladies were catching fish in the main street.

speechtext:
B.C. That is right. At that time we wondered what we would do, but the wonderful thing about it all was that there was not one single case of disease or one casualty in the area during the flooding, which lasted for three weeks, that could be traced to the flood. The waters flooded all the area taking in Dewdney, Hatzic, Nicomen island, Barnston island, Pitt Meadows, Sumas and Matsqui. Five years later in driving through some of these areas you could see the high water mark on the side of the buildings just below the eaves.
The 1950 flood in the Fraser valley was not as bad as the 1948 flood. By that time, of course, the dikes had been repaired and we also had the help of the army. I hold in my hand a booklet entitled, "Nature's Fury". It contains the stories of the newspaper reporters who saw the flood at that time and if


any hon. members are interested in looking at it there is a copy in the library. I wish I could show you some of the pictures in the booklet. This one shows where the railway and the highway were washed out at Hatzic. I do not suppose you can see it from where you sit. Here is a dead cow floating in a pasture field and here there is water up to the eaves of a barn. These are the things to which I refer.
Whose responsibility is it to see that a flood like this does not occur again? The federal and British Columbia governments have good reasons for joint participation in studies of the Fraser river development such as have been going on since 1948. The province's reasons for participation are, first, that British Columbia is concerned with flood control and hydro power. Second, the Fraser river lies wholly within the province. Third, the administration of water rights and other national resources close to the river is the responsibility of the province.
The reasons for federal participation may not be quite so readily understood, but Canada is responsible for navigation and coast and inland fisheries. This, of course, means salmon. Canada is compelled to take action whenever any national emergency occurs by flooding, the two great floods having been in 1894 and 1948. Canada is interested in hydro power development and if any such development appeared to threaten navigation and fisheries Canada would, of course, intervene.
Diking has been carried on in the lower Fraser valley for almost 100 years. At first the work was characterized by cheap construction methods and poor planning. This era reached its height at the time of the 1894 flood. The great damage done at that time certainly demonstrated that a comprehensive system of diking must be undertaken, and it was beyond the ability of private owners to finance the scheme.
Although much had been done on the building of dikes up to 1948 the great flood of that year wrecked many of the dikes. It has been said that losses totalling $20 million occurred in the lower Fraser valley flood of 1948. At that time the commander of the Canadian army in British Columbia was given control after Premier Johnson issued a proclamation declaring a state of emergency. Many agencies, including governmental, co-operated to improve the situation. When it was all over it was agreed in Ottawa that Canada would pay 75 per cent of the flood fighting costs, 75 per cent of the reconstruction costs and 50 per cent of the rehabilitation costs. The provincial government met and passed a couple of bills.

I should like to make two brief quotations from the report of the Fraser valley diking board. They had this to say:
By careful engineering methods, one can restrain the river in spots, one can nudge it here and push it there, but never, without fabulous expenditures, can the lower Fraser river be harnessed and controlled by a system of dikes. In designing this new system of dikes, the board had to compromise, striving after maximum security consistent with reasonable economics.
I think the main feature of the report of the board is the fact that dikes are not the complete answer to flood control of the Fraser river. After some study and consideration by a larger board, in 1958 the membership of the board was decreased to four members as it is now. The members from the province are the controller of water rights and the surveyor general of surveys and mappings, and from the federal government the members are the director of the water resources branch of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who is chairman, and the director of the Pacific area for the Department of Fisheries. This board has made several studies of four known ways to control floods; diking, flood detention reservoirs, river diversions and channel improvements. It seemed obvious to the board that the first two are the most effective. In the interim report presented by the board seven recommendations were made.
We should all realize at this point the enormous potential of the Fraser river basin for hydro power. We have been made aware of this aspect of the Columbia river and the Peace river in British Columbia, but what has not been emphasized is the fact that the Fraser river can produce more power than the Columbia and Peace combined, or about 45 billion kilowatt hours annually. This is about 4J times the total power presently being produced in the whole province, and does not include power already coming from the Fraser.
The preliminary report mentions three system studies by which the great majority of power could be developed. No. 2 provides the best benefit-cost and includes a power site and storage at Moran. This would create a lake 150 miles long upriver from Lillooet. However, in spite of all the fine things that can be said about a project of this nature, it cannot be undertaken because of the threat to the salmon industry. The salmon industry has an annual value of about $34 million, about $20 million goes to Canadian fishermen and the remaining $14 million to United States fishermen. It is easily understandable, therefore, that projects of the kind mentioned cannot be undertaken for power or manufacturing and flood control.
The Budget-Mr. Hicks
I will, therefore, move on to another portion of the report put out by the board. They mention four requirements for partial development. The first is to provide flood control to non-damaging levels in the lower Fraser valley. The second is to form an integral part of a comprehensive plan for the basin in which all the economical power sites would be fully developed. The third would be compatible with maintaining anadromous fish runs and the fourth to be economically selfsupporting through power production. It is worthy of note that flood control in these systems could be provided in an early stage of the development.
I should like to mention specifically at this point the lower Fraser valley dikes, some 223 miles in length. It is estimated that these dikes will withstand a flow of 375,000 cubic foot seconds of water past Hope. To build up the dikes to withstand this amount of flood would cost about $17 million with about $2 million annual in maintenance costs. So, Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes I have left I should like to give you a few quotations from some of the local newspapers emphasizing how badly they feel about the fact these dikes are not as they should be at the present time. The alternative suggestion now would be to put up storage dams in the Clearwater area.
The Agassiz Advance said:
The B.C. Progressive Conservative association, meeting in Vancouver last Friday, adopted a policy calling for an immediate start on Fraser river flood control dams as recommended by the Fraser river board.
On February 24, 1960 the Fraser Valley Record recognized that the storage dams should be built immediately to help control floods. On March 11, in the Progress, we find a note that the membership of the board of trade is expected to endorse a resolution calling on the provincial and federal governments to implement plan A recommended by the Fraser river board.
Last, but not least, the Fraser valley milk producers association which, of course, is a huge dairy co-operative in the Fraser valley with annual sales of over $27 million, passed a resolution to urge the federal and provincial governments to relieve the annual flood threat to the Fraser valley by hastening their adoption of a policy of flood control of the Fraser river which is now under study by the Fraser river board and is known as plan A. The plan, as recommended by the Fraser river board, shows that an alternative system of storage dams would be available and would not interfere with the fish runs and would, at the same time, effect the desired measure of flood control.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I just want to say that I, personally, am very much in favour of having these dams built to control the high water. I am also very much in favour of protecting our fish business in the Fraser valley in every way possible, and I am convinced both can be done successfully.

subtopic: OMER THERRIEN
speechtext: The first bill to be considered this afternoon is the petition of a 40-year old workman who has been separated from his wife since 1946. Despite humble means he has managed to bring up three children who are now in their teens. His wife has been living with another man for some time, and he is asking the House of Commons for a divorce.

subtopic: OMER THERRIEN
speechtext:
In so far as Bill No. SD-36 is concerned, the hon. member for Halifax has been kind enough to make a few comments about the circumstances surrounding it. I think this is a commendable approach because it assists in bringing to the attention of the members of the committee some of the circumstances surrounding this particular bill.
There are, however, some additional matters to those which the hon. member for Halifax has mentioned. I might point out that there are three children involved and, naturally, we should concern ourselves with their welfare. The three children are in their teens, one being 18, one 16 and the other, according to the evidence, either 15 or 14. It is possible that the birthday of the child is close to the particular date on which this evidence was given before the committee and this would account for the confusion.
The couple involved have been separated since 1946, and the children have been maintained in a boarding school by their father. There were some proceedings for separation prior to this particular petition for divorce being filed. Mr. Joyal, the counsel for the petitioner, asked some questions about this. In this instance I do not know whether Mr. Joyal is acting as agent on behalf of another

counsel who was initially retained, or whether he is the prime counsel. However, he does inquire about some separation action which was not taken by the present petitioner but by his wife, the respondent in this case. At page 11 he asks these questions of the petitioner:
Q. Has there been any action taken between you and your wife in the courts in Quebec to determine who was going to have custody of the children?
A. She took action to separate.
Q. When did she take this action?
A. I think in 1958.
Q. 1958?
A. Or 1957.
Q. Did the matter proceed to trial?
A. No.
Q. There has been nothing further done in connection with any action?
A. No.
So apparently the wife sued for separation proceedings two or three years ago but proceeded no further with that particular action. Why, I have no idea. Whether she felt she would be unable to get a favourable decision from the courts, or whether she just declined to proceed further, is open to speculation; and 1 do not think it is important in this case, except for this, that if the action for separation was taken by the wife, now the respondent in this case, and the ground alleged was adultery, it would naturally be adultery on the part of the husband who is the present petitioner. If that is the case the situation is now reversed so far as these divorce proceedings here are concerned.
If that is the case and that was the ground for the separation asked for-as I say I do not know whether it was or not, although as I understand it adultery would normally be the ground upon which one would petition or take action for separation in Quebec-perhaps there was some indication of adultery on the part of the man or the wife. But as I say, this is pure speculation.
With respect to the children there is again extensive examination.

Let us return to the evidence on page 13; I imagine this is within our rights. Evidence is again given by Charles Charron, with whom we are familiar in these cases, and his occupation is given as that of investigator. He is questioned by Mr. Joyal, and I would point out that Mr. Charron, in accordance with the ruling given in this house, makes no reference to children. He makes reference only to the things he discovered, or which it was arranged for him to discover as the case may be. I imagine that Mr. Joyal and other counsel who subsequently appear before the committee of the other place will take notice of the ruling made here that no discussion is to take place regarding children. I imagine that in future no reference will be made to the children, that we shall be as heartless and as cruel as we can in these instances. But Mr. Joyal asks Mr. Charron:
Q. I show you a photograph, which is Exhibit No. 2. Who is the person shown in that photograph?
The answer is:
A. That photograph was supplied to me by someone in the office.
The witness does not say who supplied him with the photograph. He merely says it was supplied to him. Then the evidence continues:
Q. Where did you meet Mrs.-?
I assume that though it is not made clear here, the photograph is that of the respondent. I might as well make sure, in this regard, that exhibit 2 is, in fact, shown to be a picture of the respondent as identified by the petitioner. But even though Mr. Charron does not say this, does not say that it was a photograph of the respondent, I take it we can assume it was a photograph of the respondent. Anyway, in reply to the question: "Where did you meet this woman?" an address in Montreal is given. The record continues:
Q. What date?
A. April 16, 1959.
Q. Describe to the committee the circumstances under which you saw Mrs.-at that time?
A. I was there around 5 o'clock. At 6 o'clock I saw Mr.-come in. He went into the house, so I stayed until 10.30 when I saw the light go out at 10.30. I called my assistant, Mr. Lacombe, to come and meet me, and he came at 11 o'clock and we went to the door and knocked several times before Mr.-came and opened the door slightly. When he opened the door he had on a pair of maroon pyjamas and a grey dressing gown. I walked into the bedroom then.
Q. You went into the bedroom?
A. Yes. Mrs.-was sitting in the bed and she had on a blue top of pyjamas. I asked her who she was and she admitted that she was Mrs.-. I showed her that photograph that I had, and she admitted
[The Deputy Chairman.]
it was one taken of her, so I said to the man, "You are Mr.-? You are living here as a man and wife with this lady?" He said, "Yes, what is it all about?" I told him it was divorce proceedings. He got a little mad and we went out.
I submit again that this is a highly unlikely thing to have occurred but I am sure every hon. member would agree that this situation would not normally occur. Incidentally, I point out that it is strange how often the time lag in these oases is half an hour between the time the lights go out and the time the investigators knock at the door. It is not 35 minutes, or 15 minutes; for one reason or another, it is half an hour. Perhaps it is considered that half an hour is enough time for people to have engaged in whatever they might have been engaged in after the lights went out.
According to the evidence, the two men went to the door and knocked several times before the door was opened. The man who opened the door had on a pair of pyjamas and a dressing gown. The next thing that happens is that the two men walk into the bedroom. There are no preliminaries, apparently; no pushing their way in; no explanation that they had come to check the gas meter; no question such as "how are you fixed for oil", or "how are you fixed for razor blades". They just walk through into the bedroom and find a lady sitting on the bed wearing a blue top of pyjamas.
These two complete strangers spoke to this lady who had apparently been in bed for half an hour since the lights went out. They asked her what her name was, and she said her name was so-and-so. There was no question raised: "Who are you?" or "What are you doing here?" addressed to the investigators. Then the two visitors asked another question, whether the two were living together as man and wife, and the man replied: "yes, that's right".
No one in his right mind, I submit, who is engaged in this kind of activity whether it is of a long term nature, where people are living together as man and wife, or whether it is one engagement only-and that occurs sometimes by arrangement, in divorce cases- would behave in this way. Unless these people knew that a certain thing was going to occur at eleven o'clock, or whatever time it was, and that someone was going to knock at the door, they would not open the door and allow two persons to come in and ask questions of the nature which were asked in this case, and then, only after the questions were answered, get a little mad.
I have grave doubts about this case. I submit from the evidence that was given here that what happened was this: there was some difficulty at home. The couple was

separated in 1946, as the evidence shows, and there had been trouble in the family. The two people could not get along together and in addition there was in-law trouble. Then, possibly, this woman or wife was going out with other people. These are the reasons why the divorce is sought; these are the reasons why it should be granted.
However, adultery is what we insist must occur, so couples must make arrangements accordingly. Lawyers must make arrangements, private investigators have to make arrangements either with the people concerned or with the lawyers for the sole purpose of arranging a situation where adultery might reasonably be supposed to have taken place or might have taken place. I say there is a great deal of hypocrisy about forcing people to do that sort of thing to make divorce possible when the situation is such that if they were living elsewhere- in the province of Nova Scotia, for instance- it would all be unnecessary. If these people lived in the province of Nova Scotia they could get a divorce on the basis of cruelty. If they lived in another country to which we are very close they could get a divorce on grounds of desertion. I think it is most unfair to ask that these people make these arrangements and set them up in order to meet that strict test upon which we insist, namely circumstances which could lead one to believe that adultery had taken place.
As I said before with respect to Mr. Charron, after reading and considering evidence in other cases with which we have dealt just prior to this time, these are the stereotyped answers that he gives. He knocks on the door. There is no question about what he wants or who he is. It is stated who answers the door. There is no questioning of the person who answers the door about coming in. He merely walks in, walks into the bedroom, asks whoever happens to be there what their names are. They do not hesitate to tell him "we are living as man and wife" or "this is my wife" or "this is my husband." There is no question at all about the impropriety of that sort of thing. It is just as though they had gone to a dress rehearsal in order to make sure that when they made their entrance, everything went according to plan. After it is all over, in order to give it an air of authenticity, as if these people had been disturbed, he uses this phrase "He got a little mad and we went".
I submit that it is asking the committee to stretch its imagination quite a bit to expect it to believe that this is precisely what occurred. I say this without intending any reflection upon what they concern themselves with but I submit that if the hon.
Private Bills-Divorce members of the other place had applied themselves as assiduously to examining Mr. Charron about his activities that night as they did to examining-and quite properly; I think they should examine and question on this matter-what will occur to the children after this divorce is granted, they would have found out a few other things about the adultery arrangements which probably are not shown in the particular evidence given here.
Again at the risk of incurring your wrath, Mr. Chairman, I say that the action of the Senate in the examination of the petitioner with respect to the teen-age children is an example, and is something they should do. I think the Senate should do this time and time again, regardless of these contrary rules. It shows that apparently the Senate also think the same way. It shows that they are not just concerned with rubber stamping some sort of arrangement because it meets some solemn test with respect to adultery but that they are also concerned about the welfare of other people who are affected in these particular divorce proceedings.
I may as well give you fair warning, Mr. Chairman. As I say, I do not want to incur your wrath, but I say with sincerity that, even though you have made this particular ruling, I think you should allow a fairly relaxed bit of discussion, thought and examination by members of the committee of the whole affair with respect to the children, even though the rules say something different. I hope, Mr. Chairman, I can push in that direction as much as you will allow without incurring your wrath. I would not think it would be right for members of this committee to rise on points of order, as some are wont to do from time to time, because the strict rules are not exactly followed, rules which they themselves do not follow when they are speaking about particular matters.
But when it comes to the matter of children, I think this is something with which we should concern ourselves a great deal more than we do. I submit that it is unfortunate that the jurisdiction is divided. The province itself has some jurisdiction over this matter but then we are asked to split asunder or to cut the marriage ties without concern for what certainly concerns the petitioner and the respondent, namely what occurs to the children after this divorce is granted. The children should have accorded to them far more concern and consideration than is given at the moment.

subtopic: FOREST INVENTORY, N.B.-FEDERAL PARTICIPATION
FOREST INVENTORY, N.B.-FEDERAL PARTICIPATION
speechtext:
1.	Is the federal government presently sharing the costs with the province of New Brunswick of a new forest inventory, including aerial photos?
2.	If so, what is the estimated federal cost for the completion of this inventory?
3.	What is the estimated period of time to complete this inventory?
Answer by: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
1.	Yes.
2.	An initial federal-provincial forest inventory of New Brunswick was begun in 1951 and completed in 1958 at a federal cost of $129,328. Since 1958, inventory maintenance costs have been shared under an agreement which provides for a continuing inventory progam up to March 31, 1961, when the present agreement expires. It is estimated that at that date the federal cost since April 1, 1958 will amount to a little over $51,000.
3.	See answer to part 2.
